- When sentiment is predominantly bullish (≥ 0.67) and model forecast is flat or rising slowly, adjust upward by 2–5% to account for sentiment-driven momentum.  
- If sentiment is bearish (≥ 0.67) and forecast is rising, reduce forecast by 3–8% to counteract overconfidence in upside.  
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >10% from prior period), model tends to overshoot — cap forecast increase to 2–3% per period to avoid overcorrection.  
- In high-event periods (≥15 events/30d), model often overestimates upside — apply downward bias of 5–10% to reflect supply/demand imbalance.  
- If sentiment history shows alternating bullish/bearish cycles (e.g., 0.33/1.00 alternation), model may misread trend — use 3-period moving average to smooth forecast.  
- In low-event periods (≤5 events/30d), model tends to underestimate downside — add 1–3% buffer to forecast to account for hidden volatility.  
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is low, forecast should be conservative — reduce forecast by 2–5% to avoid overestimating demand.  
- If sentiment is high but price history shows mean reversion (e.g., 3 consecutive peaks), reduce forecast slope to reflect diminishing momentum.
